doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Playing with his kids, young players, and the sounds of Hank and Elvin Jones
summary: Playing with young pianists like Leonard Thompson, he talks of the unmistakable pianist's sound of Hank Jones and of Elvin and the young drummers.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Right. Because when it gets down to that level, I don’t have any greater pleasure than I did playing with my kids. It never gets that relaxed, playing with anybody. Because we’ve just done it so often and it’s been so real and so — you know they’re your kids. So it’s a different thing. Now I played like last night, I played with this wonderful kid, Leonard Thompson. These kids, I mean I could be their grandfather actually. These kids

are maybe like 25, 30 years old, something like that. Really a great player. And the same with Jon, who is an Asian kid. But the thing is you can always tell when you’re playing with any musician, you can hear, with the piano player, the sound that he gets on the piano. Like most of these kids, well most young musicians, it might be a lot of flash and everything because a lot of young kids can do that. But there’s a sound that a jazz pianist emits and a feeling. And I always have to — what is that sound exactly? I say well anyone knows what that sound is on the piano, it’s Hank Jones. Everybody knows that. I mean Herbie Hancock even knows that. It’s just that sound, the feeling.

And with drums, I mean there’s some people like I say it’s like Elvin. Give me Elvin Jones, he’s like — he’s an old man, but he epitomizes like my era of drummers. Not that these kids aren’t playing — I don’t know if you know some of these guys like Billy Kilson and Billy Drummond and Gregory Hutchinson, these are these young kids that are demon drummers. And all of us, as soon as we listen to Elvin we have to go — and Max is another one. Still going. Max was at my house a couple of years ago, he was in town doing a recording so I invited him over the house. I had my drums set up in the living room and he sits down to play and I’m playing the piano and we’re playing these blues and everything. And he’s singing.
